# Doefin brand context

Every rule for writing and designing for Doefin, in one file. Follow it for any Doefin copy, post, email, newsletter, deck, document, glossary entry or interface. Where files below disagree, compliance wins, then voice.


<!-- source: brand/overview.md -->
## Doefin brand: overview

How Doefin looks and how it writes, on the website, in the app, on X and LinkedIn, in email and in decks. The writing matters most. If you read one file, read `voice.md`. If you write anything long, read `matteo/thinking.md` too.

### Doefin in one line

**Trade and hedge Bitcoin hashrate exposure through markets on mining difficulty.**

When there is room for more, in Matteo's words: Doefin provides markets for trading and hedging Bitcoin hashrate exposure. Our contracts reference future Bitcoin mining difficulty. We help miners assess that exposure and give professional investors a way to trade their views through defined market outcomes.

How a market works, in one sentence: each market asks whether difficulty will be at or above a set level at a specified Bitcoin block, and positions are funded and settled in cbBTC.

Hashrate is what people are exposed to; difficulty decides the contract. Do not call Doefin "hashrate derivatives" or a "prediction market".

Company line for footers, documents and decks: Doefin, Port Louis, Mauritius.

### Who we write for

Miners and the people who finance them, and funds and trading desks. All of them are professional investors. They know mining and check the maths. They stop reading at the first line of hype. We never write for retail readers.

Miners hedge; investors and desks trade a view. Name each reader and what it does, rather than writing for everyone at once.

### The short version

- `ink` and white do most of the work. Doefin Blue marks the one thing to look at.
- Flat colour. No gradients, glows or frosted glass.
- Manrope for everything, with figures that line up in columns.
- Numbers come with their unit, and with a date and a source whenever they can change.
- Short sentences, real numbers and the qualifiers that make them true. Write it the way Matteo would explain it to a miner.
- No contractions.
- Use the logo files as they are. Never redraw, stretch or recolour them.

### Before anything goes out

- Does the first line get straight to the subject?
- Is every number exact, with its unit, its date and its qualifier?
- If it says what Doefin lets people do, does it say what can go wrong, next to the claim?
- Did it pass the copy checker (`tools/check_copy.py`)?
- Is it free of promises, real returns and anything aimed at retail?
- Does it contain one of the five kinds Matteo reviews first (`compliance.md`)? Then send it to him.

## How we write

We write the way Matteo explains Doefin to someone who knows mining. The point comes first, then the number with the qualifiers that make it true. When the piece is about Doefin, it also says what the reader can do and what that will not do. We do not oversell.

For how he reasons, with his own rewrites as evidence, read `matteo/thinking.md` and `matteo/edits.md`.

### The habits

- The first line is plain and gets straight to the subject: a number, a claim he will defend, or the reader's question. "A 5.92% rise in difficulty means about 5.6% less expected BTC production at the same hashrate, all else equal." "Difficulty exposure makes Bitcoin mining businesses unbankable."
- Keep sentences short, with one idea each. On X, put one sentence on each line. On LinkedIn, use short paragraphs of one to three sentences. Split anything over 30 words.
- Use real numbers, and do the arithmetic: for a difficulty change d, expected production changes by 1/(1 + d) − 1 (a 10% rise gives −9.1%). Give the figure, the unit and the date: "+5.9% adjustment (16 Oct)". Mark an estimate as one: "about +4.7%", "~10%". A forecast comes with its range.
- Keep the qualifiers that make a number true: expected, at the same hashrate, all else equal.
- Hashrate is the exposure; difficulty decides the contract. Say it once per piece.
- Name each reader and what it does: miners hedge, investors and desks trade a view.
- Say what can go wrong next to the claim: "A difficulty position may offset some exposure, but it does not cover every risk in a mining business."
- Name the trade-off in arguments too: "That 4x multiple is gross revenue, not net margin."
- On the website, tell the reader what to do, with a verb: "Choose a market. Fund your account. Place a trade." A market update needs no call to action.
- Say a thing once.
- Mark an opinion as yours ("I think", "from what we have seen so far") and keep it apart from company facts. Give a fact its source.
- Borrow a comparison the reader already knows. Matteo explains benchmarks with WTI and Brent. A good comparison saves a paragraph.

### Matteo's lines

These come from his posts and his rewrites. When a draft feels off, read them again.

> Few talk about Bitcoin hashrate.

> Trade and hedge Bitcoin hashrate exposure through markets on mining difficulty.

> Hashrate is the economic exposure; difficulty determines the contract outcome.

> A 5.92% rise in difficulty means about 5.6% less expected BTC production at the same hashrate, all else equal.

> That 4x multiple is gross revenue, not net margin.

> So yes, "AI pays more", but it also costs more.

> Choose a market. Fund your account. Place a trade.

> You can lose the full amount paid for a position.

> That distinction matters. A difficulty position may offset some exposure, but it does not cover every risk in a mining business or a loan.

> Bitcoin compute (hashrate) has an advantage here: one global network, one difficulty adjustment mechanism and a benchmark everyone can verify.

They open plainly, use exact figures with their qualifiers, turn on a "But" or a "So yes", state the limit and end on one point.

### What generated copy sounds like

Readers spot machine-written copy within a line. After that they stop trusting the numbers. Cut these.

Words: delve, leverage, utilise, seamless, robust, cutting-edge, next-generation, game-changing, revolutionary, transformative, unlock, unleash, empower, elevate, harness, supercharge, landscape, ever-evolving, fast-paced, holistic, synergy, myriad, plethora, tapestry, testament, pivotal, crucial, moreover, furthermore, additionally, notably, ultimately.

Openings: "In today's…", "In the world of…", "When it comes to…", "Whether you're a miner or a fund…", "Let's dive in", "Here's the thing".

Shapes:

- Em dashes around an aside. Use a full stop, a comma or brackets.
- Empty contrasts: "It's not just a market, it's a movement." A contrast between two facts is fine: "gross revenue, not net margin".
- Teaser questions answered in the next breath: "The result? …" A real question the reader would ask is fine: "How much does difficulty change your expected Bitcoin production?"
- A bold label at the start of every bullet.
- A last line that repeats the post: "In short…", "Ultimately…".
- Hashtags, and emoji used as decoration.

### Rewrites

| Generated | Ours |

| In today's fast-evolving mining landscape, difficulty volatility presents both challenges and opportunities. | A 5.92% rise in difficulty means about 5.6% less expected BTC production at the same hashrate, all else equal. |
| Doefin empowers miners to seamlessly navigate network risk with cutting-edge on-chain tools. | Miners can hedge the effect of rising difficulty on expected Bitcoin production. |
| It's not just a market. It's a new way to think about hashrate. | Cut it. |
| We're thrilled to announce our groundbreaking launch! 🚀 | Doefin goes live tomorrow. |
| Whether you're a miner, a lender or a fund, we've got you covered. | Miners can hedge the effect of rising difficulty. Investors can trade their views on network hashrate. |
| Take a closer look at Doefin. | Put your hashrate view to work. |
| Production protection | Estimate BTC production |
| I hope this email finds you well. I wanted to reach out about a potential synergy. | Spoke to Dan from Luxor. He had an idea I would like your view on. |

### Names, numbers and dates

- Doefin with a capital D in all text. DOEFIN is the logo only. Lower case only in web addresses and handles.
- Bitcoin for the network, always with a capital B. BTC for amounts: 0.25 BTC.
- cbBTC, explained the first time: a wrapped Bitcoin asset; it is not native BTC.
- hashrate and hashprice are one word, lower case.
- Difficulty adjustment: every 2,016 blocks, about two weeks. Use "epoch" only after you have explained it.
- Yes and No, in sentence case, when they name a side of a market. Never "YES/NO position". In marketing copy, describe the position instead: "a position that pays out if difficulty is above X" (an open question for Matteo, `decisions.md`).
- Difficulty in T with no space: 140.58T. Other units take a space: 1.2 ZH/s, 0.05 BTC. No space before %: 5.9%. Percentage points as pp: 4.67 pp.
- Give a change its sign (+5.9%, −3.0%) unless a word like rose or fell already says which way it went. Use the real minus sign (−).
- Dates: 16 Oct 2026. Drop the year when it is this year. No "16th", no 10/16.
- Block heights with a comma: block 971,712.
- Share prices as decimals: 0.45. Money with its currency: $36, 0.25 BTC.
- Ranges with an en dash: 10–15 years.

### Grammar

- British spelling, as on the website and in Matteo's posts: stabilise, collateralised, colour, behaviour.
- Sentence case for headings, buttons, titles and subject lines. Internal emails can use capital section labels, as Matteo's do.
- No contractions: "I am", "you are", "there is", "do not", "it is". This is Matteo's rule, for every channel.
- Start a sentence with But or So when that is how you would say it.
- No serial comma, unless a list is unclear without it.
- "We" is Doefin and "you" is the reader. Matteo's own posts say "I".

## How Matteo thinks when he writes

Matteo Spinosa is Doefin's CEO. This file describes how he reasons when he writes, so that a person or a model can produce a first draft he would sign without rewriting it.

It is built from three sources. Each pattern below cites one of them.

- His public posts (`../voice-samples.md`).
- His rewrites of 37 of our drafts in the tone check of 29 Oct 2026 (`edits.md`, cited as E01 to E37).
- The rules he wrote down in the same tone check ("Rules in his own words" in `edits.md`).

Two limits on the evidence. His internal email about an auction mode says he asked Claude and ChatGPT to help draft it, so it is not used as evidence of his voice. Some of his tone-check rule answers read more polished than his notes ("Hmmm, maybe yes."); they may have been drafted with help, so treat their wording as his position rather than his style.

Where an older post and the tone check disagree, the tone check wins, because it is newer. His launch posts quoted a return and said "Buy YES". In the tone check he asked to avoid "the YES/NO position" and listed performance claims among what he reviews before anything goes out.

A habit below is backed by his own statement or by at least three edits. Anything thinner waits under "Seen in his edits, not yet confirmed" at the end.

### What he is doing when he writes

He explains an exposure to a professional who will check the maths. A piece usually answers some of these, in this order:

1. What is true, or what moved? A number, a mechanism or a claim he will defend.
2. What does it do to the reader's production or money? That is the exposure.
3. When the piece is about Doefin: what can the reader do, and what will that not do?

Not every piece needs all three. His X update (E35) states a number and why it matters, with no call to action. Do not invent one.

### His habits of mind

#### 1. Exposures, not features

He starts from what the reader is exposed to, then says what Doefin lets them do about it.

- "Miners can hedge the effect of rising difficulty on expected Bitcoin production. Investors can trade their views on network hashrate…" (E14)
- "The key risk is not only BTC price. It is also network hashrate and difficulty, which directly determine Bitcoin miners revenues." (post on mining and AI)
- "Network growth changes miners' production exposure." (E35)

Hashrate is the economic exposure. Difficulty is the public number that decides the contract. He keeps the two apart, and asked for the distinction to be clear "without repeating the full explanation in every section". In his words: "Hashrate is the economic exposure; difficulty determines the contract outcome." (E23)

#### 2. He names each reader and what it does

Miners hedge; investors and desks trade a view (E08, E09, E14, E32). Sometimes in two sentences (E14), sometimes in one ("We help miners assess that exposure and give professional investors a way to trade their views", E32). "Whether you are a miner or a fund" never appears in his writing.

#### 3. Precise beats punchy

When a draft rounds a number or uses a casual word, he puts the qualifier back.

- "about 5.6% fewer coins" became "about 5.6% less expected BTC production at the same hashrate, all else equal" (E06, E35).
- "about 9% fewer coins" became "about 9.1% less expected BTC production" (E36). The arithmetic: for a difficulty change d, expected production changes by 1/(1 + d) − 1. A 10% rise gives 1/1.10 − 1 = −9.1%. A 3.2% fall gives 1/0.968 − 1 = +3.3%.
- "inferred … rather than read from a register of mining machines" became "estimated from difficulty and block timing. It is not a direct count of Bitcoin mining machines." (E30)
- "Difficulty is the dial that holds that average steady" became a definition with its reference and a formula: "difficulty × 2³² ÷ 600 hashes per second" (E29).

His qualifiers: expected, at the same hashrate, all else equal, about, ~, approximately, an estimate, not a live measurement.

#### 4. He states the downside himself, next to the claim

He does not leave risk to a footer. In the tone check he added risk lines to our drafts:

- "You can lose the full amount paid for a position." (E17, E34)
- "A difficulty position may offset some mining losses, but does not cover every source of production or revenue risk." (E17)
- "Execution depends on available liquidity and price, so a full exit is not guaranteed." (E16)
- "Trading involves the risk of loss." (E22)
- "That distinction matters. A difficulty position may offset some exposure, but it does not cover every risk in a mining business or a loan." (E36)

His posts do the same with arguments: "That 4x multiple is gross revenue, not net margin." "So yes, 'AI pays more', but it also costs more."

Never remove one of these lines to satisfy the checker. A risk line is always needed.

#### 5. Verbs and a next action, in product copy

On the website, he tells the reader what to do.

- "Choose a market. Fund your account. Place a trade." (E15)
- "Put your hashrate view to work." with the buttons "Enter app" and "Contact the team" (E19)
- "Production protection" became "Estimate BTC production" (E21).
- "Use Doefin markets to hedge that exposure." (E08) "Use Doefin's production calculator…" (E37)

He replaced descriptions with these actions: "Take a closer look at Doefin." (E12, E19), "Review both outcomes before entering." (E07, E15).

#### 6. Say it once

His words: "We already had point 3 … why we need to repeat again?" (E24). "Too much information. Not needed (already in point 3 'how it works')." (E25). And his rule: keep the hashrate and difficulty distinction clear "without repeating the full explanation in every section".

#### 7. Verifiable is the reason

When Doefin needs a reason to exist, this is the one he gives: difficulty is public and anyone can check it.

- "one global network, one difficulty adjustment mechanism and a benchmark everyone can verify" (post on AI compute)
- "giving your hashrate view a publicly verifiable reference" (E22)
- "Difficulty gives that exposure a public, verifiable reference." (E35)
- "so the outcome is defined and publicly verifiable" (E36)

#### 8. Frames from markets the reader knows

WTI and Brent for benchmarks. Italian utilities against Italian industrials. AI landlord deals against mining revenue per MW. One comparison, made carefully ("Okay, oil is not uniform either, but…"), then back to Bitcoin.

#### 9. A claim he will defend

His opinion pieces open on a sentence someone could argue with: "Difficulty exposure makes Bitcoin mining businesses unbankable." (E36) "Few talk about Bitcoin hashrate." "Bitcoin mining and AI are increasingly competing for the same resource: the energized megawatt." Then he earns it: the mechanism, one worked number, "I think", what Doefin does, and the limit.

#### 10. Plain register, no contractions

- No contractions, ever: "I am", "you are", "there is", "do not". He asked for this in so many words.
- Conversational where it helps: "Okay, …", "So yes, …", "superstars".
- He turns an argument with "But", "So yes" or "Okay, … but".
- He marks opinion and keeps it apart from company fact: "I think", "From what we have seen so far". His rule: "Separate personal opinion from company facts."
- Warm and specific when he thanks people. He names them and says what they did and what it meant. Then one humble line: "I wish Doefin were at a later stage so that I could already be giving back".

#### 11. His words, and the words he will not use

Words he asked for: trade, hedge, hashrate exposure, mining difficulty, expected BTC production, market terms, position cost and payout, and "shares" in customer copy, explained once as position tokens.

Words he used in his rewrites: threshold, settlement block, specified block, payout, cbBTC (explained once: "a wrapped Bitcoin asset; it is not native BTC").

Never, in his words: "guaranteed profit", "risk-free", "protect all revenues", "native yield". Never imply that a position directly delivers hashrate or covers every mining risk.

### How each kind of writing is built

| Kind | His shape | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Market update (X) | The number, with its qualifiers. What it does to production. Why it matters: exposure, and a public reference. No call to action. | E35 |
| Opinion (LinkedIn) | A claim he will defend. The mechanism. One worked number. "I think". Where Doefin fits. The limit. | E36, post on mining and AI |
| Product update | The reader's question. The tool that answers it. Where to find it. | E37 |
| Website and product copy | An action headline. Who does what (miners hedge, investors trade). The mechanics in one sentence. The risk line. A button with a verb. | E13, E14, E19, E22 |
| Help and docs | Imperatives, then steps, each with its limit. The rule stated, not the waiting described. Risks as a labelled list. | E15, E25, E27 |
| Glossary | The technical definition. How it adjusts. What it does to production. Related measures, each with what it is not. | E29 |
| Tool text | What the tool estimates. Inputs with units. Assumptions shown. Production kept apart from revenue and profit. Results called estimates, with their limits near them. | E28, his rule on tool text |
| Partner and investor emails | Why I am writing. Then (1) what happened and deal flow, (2) what I am thinking, (3) idea or next steps, (4) product updates, (5) the ask. | His rule on emails |
| Thank-you | Name the people. Say what they did and what it meant. One humble line. Thank them by name. | QUBIC post |

His lines are examples of a move, not templates. Do not reuse "Difficulty gives that exposure a public, verifiable reference" in every post; make the same move in new words.

### Before you hand a draft over, ask what Matteo would ask

1. Who is speaking: the company ("we") or Matteo ("I")?
2. What is the exposure, and whose is it?
3. Is every number exact, with its unit and its qualifier (expected, at the same hashrate, all else equal)? Did I do the arithmetic with 1/(1 + d) − 1?
4. Is hashrate the exposure and difficulty what decides the contract, said once?
5. If the piece says what Doefin lets people do: did I say what can go wrong, next to the claim?
6. Have I already said this somewhere else on the page? Cut it.
7. On the website: does the reader know what to do next, in a verb?
8. Could any line read as a promise?
9. Is any line a new product claim, settlement or collateral wording, a financial example (a price, cost, payout or profit for a position), a performance claim, or legal or access language? Those go to Matteo first. A production estimate in BTC is not a financial example.
10. Is there a contraction left anywhere?

### How this file grows

Every new edit from Matteo goes into `edits.md`, using the learner procedure in `skills/doefin-voice/SKILL.md`. A pattern becomes a habit above when Matteo states it, or when it shows up in three separate edits. Until then it waits below. Where his own writing disagrees with itself, the question goes to the Open table in `../decisions.md`, not here.

### Seen in his edits, not yet confirmed

- Worked examples instead of advice: once, where we asked (E26). Never invent figures for one; use placeholders, and a worked payout example always goes to Matteo.
- "Retarget" did not survive his edits (E18, E31). He writes "difficulty adjustment".
- In customer copy he wrote "threshold" and "settlement block" or "specified block" (E15, E22, E25), although his launch post said "strike" and "expiry block".
- He cut a line that sent the reader to the team for company details (E33), with no comment. Elsewhere he added "talk to the team" himself (E19).
- He cut "A threshold. An observation. A binary outcome." because it repeated How it works (E24). His own launch post ends on fragments ("Built for institutions. Collateralised in Bitcoin, settled on energy."), so fragments as such are not banned.

- He made the opinion post longer than our draft (E36), while asking for about 100 words for updates.

## What we cannot say

Doefin is registered in Port Louis, Mauritius, and is for professional investors only. Anything that invites someone to trade counts as a financial promotion, and those are tightly regulated. So:

- Do not write for retail readers. Avoid "anyone can trade", "for everyone" and "beginners".
- Never promise an outcome. No "guaranteed profit", "risk-free", "protect all revenues" or "native yield". Never imply that a position delivers hashrate or covers every mining risk.
- Never post a real or past return, or a past trade's gain. A worked payout example (one is in Matteo's own docs rewrite, E26) is labelled illustrative, shows the loss as plainly as the win, gives the position cost and the payout before fees, and says that a payout includes the amount paid and is not all profit. Every one goes to Matteo. Never make up figures for one; use placeholders.
- "Hedge" describes what Doefin lets miners do. Where there is room, say what it does not cover: "A difficulty position may offset some exposure, but it does not cover every risk in a mining business." Never say a named miner or fund uses Doefin unless it is true and they agreed.
- Never call anything "AI-powered". Forecasting difficulty is arithmetic.
- Give every number that can change a dated source. Mark anything single-source or a judgement as such.
- Name peers and competitors only in relevant, factual comparisons backed by current evidence. Never imply endorsement or affiliation.
- A screenshot of live prices shows, if possible, its date and time, the market and the quote units. Never imply that a quote guarantees execution, liquidity or a return.
- Pages, decks, documents, the newsletter footer and any post about Doefin markets or positions end with the disclaimer: "Doefin is for professional investors only. You can lose the full amount paid for a position. Nothing here is investment advice." This is a house rule, not Matteo's: his rewrites of posts carried none, so which posts need it is an open question (`decisions.md`).

### What goes to Matteo before it goes out

Doefin has not named a compliance approver yet (see `decisions.md`). Until it does, Matteo reviews these before they are published:

- new product claims;
- changes to settlement or collateral wording;
- financial examples, including worked payout examples;
- performance claims;
- legal or access language.

A production estimate in BTC is not a financial example; a price, cost, payout or profit for a position is. His rule for everything else: "Routine content should use the agreed wording." Whether that means it can skip his review is still open (`decisions.md`). When you are not sure, send it to him.

The copy checker marks the words he will want to see as `CHECK`. List them for him when you send a draft.

## Rules for each kind of content

Matteo reviewed these in the tone check on 29 Oct 2026. Where he added to a rule, his words are in. Where he left a rule blank, it stands as drafted.

All of them sit on top of `voice.md` and `compliance.md`. `matteo/thinking.md` shows how he builds each kind.

### Slides and decks

- One message per slide, written as a full-sentence title.
- One big number at most per slide.
- A source line on every slide with data.
- Ink title slide, white content slides. Start from the deck template (`links.md`).
- Investor and partner decks follow the same standards for evidence, product mechanics and risk. Change the depth and emphasis for the audience, not the standards.

### Company posts on X and LinkedIn

- The point or the number first, then two or three short lines, then the view.
- No hashtags. Emoji and exclamation marks only when they fit. The account says "we".
- LinkedIn: up to 250 words when the post explains an argument; about 100 words for an update, which is the preference.
- Live prices from the app, if possible as dated, time-stamped screenshots with the market and quote units visible. Never a hint that a quote guarantees execution, liquidity or a return. Never a gain (house rule).

### Matteo's own posts

- His voice and "I". Personal opinion kept apart from company facts.
- The same standards for numbers, product claims and risk wording as company posts.
- The agreed product language, used the same way every time.

### Newsletter

- Lead with the news and explain why it matters.
- Cover difficulty markets, trading activity and network hashrate.
- Link the sources and date every estimate.
- A factual subject line.
- State a publishing cadence only when the team has committed to one.
- Include the relevant risk context whenever an issue discusses positions.
- Signed Doefin. A piece that gives a personal view names its author.

### Glossary

- A plain, factual definition under 160 characters, with no product language.
- Then a longer explanation and one worked example.
- For a measure, say what it is not as well as what it is ("not a live measurement of mining activity").

### Research notes and articles

- State the main finding early.
- Give every figure its source, date, units and method.
- Keep observations, estimates, forecasts and opinion apart, and label each. The website's source badges (Measured, Single source, Judgement, Illustrative) still apply to each figure.
- Explain the assumptions and any material uncertainty.
- Assess forecast hits and misses with the same method, and make material misses and corrections visible.

### Help docs

- "You", short steps, one task per page.
- A warning comes before the step it affects.
- Explain a rule rather than describing the wait ("Yes wins if the difficulty at that block is at or above the threshold").

### Tool text

- Say what the tool estimates.
- Label every input with its unit, and show the assumptions.
- Explain the result in plain language, and keep BTC production apart from revenue and profit.
- Call outputs estimates, and show their material limitations next to the result.

### Emails to partners and investors

- Open with the reason for writing, give the context they need, and end with one clear ask.
- An update can follow Matteo's order: (1) what happened, and deal flow; (2) what I am thinking; (3) the idea or next steps; (4) product updates, if any; (5) the ask.
- Signed with a first name.

### Announcements

- What changed, for whom and from when.
- No "thrilled" and no "game-changing". A claim like "first" needs proof on file.

### App text

- Buttons start with a verb. The app button on the website says "Enter app".
- Errors say what happened and what to do next.
- Confirmations repeat the button's words.

## Website and app

The site has four sections (Product, Tools, Data & Research, Learn) and an Enter app button.

- Headings say what the reader gets or does, in under eight words: "Trade and hedge Bitcoin hashrate exposure." "Put your hashrate view to work."
- Buttons start with a verb and say what happens: "Enter app", "Estimate BTC production", "Contact the team". Never "Learn more", "Click here" or "Submit".
- One sentence for each reader: miners hedge the effect of rising difficulty on expected production; investors trade their views on network hashrate.
- Say how a market works once, in the How it works section. Other sections link to it rather than repeat it.
- Data pages put the number first, with its unit, its date and a source badge: Measured, Single source, Judgement or Illustrative. Each grade is defined in `visual.md` under Badges.
- Any made-up or sample figure carries the Illustrative badge.
- Every chart has its numbers in the caption underneath.
- Error messages say what went wrong and what to do next: "Order not placed. This market is closed. Choose an open market."
- Every page ends with the footer, in Matteo's words: "Trade and hedge Bitcoin hashrate exposure through markets on mining difficulty. For professional investors. You can lose the full amount paid for a position. Nothing here is investment advice."
- Risk sits next to the claim as well as in the footer: "Trading involves the risk of loss." FAQs and docs list the risks by name (position, exit, collateral and technical, hedge limitations).
- Every article gets a share card at 1200 × 630: a label, the title and the wordmark. It is the picture people see when the link is shared on LinkedIn, X or Slack.
- Dark theme, `bg` ground, one `action` button per view.


<!-- source: brand/channels/social.md -->
## X and LinkedIn

- Profile picture: `doefin-icon-blue.png`. Headers: `x-header-1500x500.png` and `linkedin-cover-1128x191.png`, in `assets/social/`.
- Bio: "Trade and hedge Bitcoin hashrate exposure through markets on mining difficulty. For professional investors."
- LinkedIn About: "Doefin provides markets for trading and hedging Bitcoin hashrate exposure." Then, if there is room: "Our contracts reference future Bitcoin mining difficulty. We help miners assess that exposure and give professional investors a way to trade their views through defined market outcomes."
- Write posts the way Matteo does. The first line is the number, a claim or the reader's question. Then the figures and what they mean, with their qualifiers. The last line is the view or the limit.
- On X, one sentence per line. On LinkedIn, short paragraphs of one to three sentences: up to 250 words for an argument, about 100 for an update.
- When a post needs a chart or more than a few paragraphs, write it as an article on the website. Then post the main number with the link.
- A post with a number uses the figure card: one number, its label, its date and its source. 1200 × 675 fits both X and LinkedIn.
- A post from the app uses the app screenshot template: the screen, a one-line headline and the capture date and time, with the market and quote units visible. Crop to the part that makes the point. Never show a gain or a return, or suggest a quote guarantees execution.
- A LinkedIn carousel has three to five portrait pages: the question, the arithmetic, then the source and the disclaimer.
- Posts about Doefin markets or positions end with the disclaimer (house rule; which posts need it is open in `../decisions.md`). A post only about network data does not.
- The company account says "we". Matteo says "I".
- Emoji and exclamation marks only when they fit. No hashtags, no tagging people for reach.
- Name peers only in factual comparisons backed by current evidence.


<!-- source: brand/channels/email.md -->
## Email and newsletter

- Subject lines carry the news in plain words, in under 50 characters and in sentence case: "Difficulty up 5.92% on 16 Oct".
- The newsletter leads with the news and why it matters, then covers difficulty markets, trading activity and network hashrate, each with its source and dated estimates. Risk context goes in wherever positions are discussed. It is signed Doefin and closes with the disclaimer and an unsubscribe link. Do not promise a cadence until the team has committed to one.
- Outreach follows Matteo's pattern. The first line says why you are writing. Two or three sentences give the context. Then ask for one thing. Sign with a first name.
- Updates to partners and investors follow his order: what happened and deal flow, what I am thinking, the idea or next steps, product updates if any, then the ask.
- Requests to the team can follow the shape of his auction email: the goal in one sentence, then sections with capital labels (HOW IT WORKS, TIMING, PLEASE CONFIRM), ending with the questions you need answered. He says that email was drafted with an assistant's help, so treat the shape as a format, not as his voice.
- Never write "I hope this finds you well", "Just following up", "I wanted to reach out", "Quick question" or "circle back".
- Only email people who have agreed to hear from us, and keep a record of when and how they agreed.


<!-- source: brand/channels/decks.md -->
## Decks

- Start every deck from the Doefin Deck Template.
- One message per slide, written as the slide title in a full sentence: "Difficulty rose 12.5% since its June low." Never "Market overview".
- Title, section and closing slides are `ink` with the white wordmark. Content slides are white, with `text` and one `blue` highlight.
- At most one big number per slide, in `figure-xl`.
- Every slide with data has a source line at the bottom, in `small` and `text-muted`: "Source: mempool.space, fetched 27 Oct 2026."
- Four bullets at most. If you need more, write a document instead.
- Investor and partner decks hold the same standards for evidence, product mechanics and risk; only the depth changes.
- The closing slide carries the disclaimer.

## Documents

- Reports and one-pagers start from the Documents page of Doefin Templates and export as PDF.
- A report opens with the `ink` cover: the wordmark, the title and the month. Inner pages are white, with the ink wordmark at the top.
- Each inner page ends with the disclaimer and a page number.
- Charts and tables follow the Chart rules: the numbers in a caption, the source underneath.
- Light theme, Manrope and sentence-case headings throughout.


<!-- source: brand/visual.md -->
## Visual identity

Colour, type and spacing values live in `tokens/tokens.json`; `dist/tokens.css` and `dist/tailwind-preset.cjs` are built from it. Token names in backticks below are those tokens.

### Logo

The wordmark is DOEFIN in slanted capitals. The inside of the D is a fin. Always use the files in `assets/logos/`. Never set the name in a font as a stand-in.

| Ground | Wordmark | File |
|---|---|---|
| `ink`, or any dark ground | White | `doefin-wordmark-white.svg` |
| `white`, light `bg`, or any light ground | Ink | `doefin-wordmark-ink.svg` |
| `blue` | White | `doefin-wordmark-white.svg` |

- Keep clear space around the wordmark equal to half its height, on every side.
- Minimum size: 80px wide on screen, 20 mm in print. Smaller than that, use the icon.
- The icon is the D on its own: white on `blue` (`doefin-icon-blue.svg`), or white on `ink` (`doefin-icon-ink.svg`). Use it wherever a square is needed: profile pictures, the app icon, the favicon.
- Do not stretch it, rotate it or straighten the slant. Do not add outlines, shadows or gradients.
- On a photo or a busy background, put the wordmark on a flat `ink` or `blue` panel.

### Colour

Most of any layout is `ink` and white. Doefin Blue (`blue`) marks the one thing to look at: the main number, the main line in a chart, one block of colour. Use `blue` for one thing per screen. Buttons, links and the faint big letter do not count.

Dark is home: the app, the website and social images. Light is for documents, decks, PDFs and print.

| Job | Tokens |
|---|---|
| Page ground | `bg` |
| Cards and panels | `surface`, `surface-alt`, edged with `line` |
| Text | `text`; `text-muted` for labels, dates and sources |
| Links | `link` |
| Primary button | `action` with `on-action` text, once per view |
| Gains and losses | `up` and `down`, always with a sign or an arrow |
| Warnings and the Illustrative badge | `caution` with `on-caution` text |
| Charts | `chart-1`, `chart-2`, `chart-context`, `chart-band` |

- `up` and `down` mean gain and loss on a position or a price. A rise in difficulty is not a gain: show it in `text` with its sign.
- Never use orange as decoration. On a trading screen it reads as a loss.
- Use flat colour. No gradients, glows or frosted-glass panels.
- Use `blue` as text only at 24px and up. Smaller links use `link`; buttons use `action`.

No longer in use: the blue-to-purple gradient and the pink and purple glows; #5B73E8, #4F85F6 and #CCEAFB (use `blue`); #838EA7 (use `text-muted`); orange eyebrows and icons (use `text-muted` or `blue`).

### Type

Manrope for everything, from Regular (400) to ExtraBold (800).

- `display` for title slides and social cards. `title-1`, `title-2` and `title-3` for headings.
- `body` in the app. `body-lg` for anything longer than a paragraph. `small` for captions, sources and the disclaimer.
- `label` for eyebrows (the small line above a heading) and column heads, set in capitals.
- `figure-xl` and `figure` for the main numbers. `mono` only for addresses and hashes.

Rules:

- Sentence case for every heading, button and title.
- Figures line up in columns. Developers set `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` on every number.
- Manrope has no italic, so do not press the italic button: the software will fake a slant. Use bold for emphasis, and use it rarely.
- Keep reading text narrower than `measure`.
- In Google Slides and Google Docs, choose Manrope from the font menu. In PowerPoint or Word without Manrope installed, use Arial.

### Layout and shape

- Spacing comes from the scale: `space-4` is the phone gutter, `space-6` sits inside and between cards, `space-16` sits between sections on desktop.
- Corners: `radius-panel` on cards and panels, `radius-md` on buttons and inputs, `radius-sm` on badges, `radius-pill` on gain and loss chips.
- Separate things with space first and a `line` hairline second. Only menus, popovers and tooltips get `shadow-float`.
- Page content stays inside `container`.

### The big letters

One letter of the wordmark, usually the D, can sit very large behind a layout: `blue` at 6% to 14% opacity, cropped by the edge. One letter per layout, never the whole word as a pattern. Slanted shapes use the wordmark's angle, `slant`, and no other.

### Charts

- Our series is `chart-1`. Everything else is `chart-context` grey. Use `chart-2` only when a second series needs its own colour, and label both lines on the chart.
- A forecast always shows its range as a `chart-band`, and the caption gives the range in numbers.
- Every chart has its numbers in a caption: the start, the end, the high or low, the dates and the source. A reader who cannot see the chart still gets the point.
- 2px lines, hairline grid, one y-axis. No 3D and no animation on load.
- Difficulty adjustments are bars above or below zero in one colour. `up` and `down` stay for money.

### Icons

Line icons on a 24px grid, 2px stroke, round ends, no fill. Colour them `text-muted`, or `blue` for the one active item. No emoji in the app, on the website or in email. On social, only when it fits.

### Images

Use what is real: charts of real data, app screenshots with the date visible, photos of real people and real mining sites. No stock photos, no 3D coins, no rockets, no glowing networks, no AI-generated pictures.

### Badges

Source grades on any figure:

- Measured: read from a public source, like the Bitcoin chain or mempool.space.
- Single source: one source only, not checked against another.
- Judgement: our view. Shown with a dashed border.
- Illustrative: sample data, not live. Every made-up or placeholder number carries it, on a `caution` fill.

Gain and loss chips use `up` and `down`, always with a sign and an arrow, and only for money.

<!-- source: brand/voice-samples.md -->
## Matteo's writing: voice samples

Public posts by Matteo Spinosa, CEO, kept as a reference for how Doefin sounds. Read them before drafting anything long. Imitate the rhythm and the reasoning, not the content: the figures were true on the day he posted.

The first three are his rewrites from the tone check (29 Oct 2026), the newest and closest to what he wants now. The rest are older posts. One of those uses a contraction ("That's"); since the tone check, his rule is no contractions, so do not copy it.

Left out on purpose: internal emails (`matteo/thinking.md` describes the shape of one), and posts that quote a trade's return or invite people to trade (see `compliance.md`). His rewrites of website copy are in `matteo/edits.md`.

### LinkedIn: lenders and difficulty (tone check rewrite)

Difficulty exposure makes Bitcoin mining businesses unbankable.

When a loan depends on future Bitcoin production, Bitcoin difficulty affects the assumptions behind repayment. For example, a 10% difficulty rise means about 9.1% less expected BTC production at the same hashrate, all else equal.

I think lenders have a reason to watch this market. A price for future difficulty allows them to estimate future Bitcoin miners' revenues.

Doefin's proposition is trading and hedging hashrate exposure. Its contracts reference difficulty, so the outcome is defined and publicly verifiable.

That distinction matters. A difficulty position may offset some exposure, but it does not cover every risk in a mining business or a loan.

### LinkedIn: a product update (tone check rewrite)

How much does difficulty change your expected Bitcoin production?

Use Doefin's production calculator to compare difficulty scenarios at your fleet's hashrate.

Explore the calculator on the Doefin website.

### X: a difficulty adjustment (tone check rewrite)

A 5.92% rise in difficulty means about 5.6% less expected BTC production at the same hashrate, all else equal.

Network growth changes miners' production exposure. Difficulty gives that exposure a public, verifiable reference.

### X: a benchmark for compute

Many companies are building derivatives on AI compute.

But AI compute remains fragmented: different chips, models, regions, performance benchmarks and verification methods.

Okay, oil is not uniform either, but WTI and Brent became the benchmarks around which enormous derivatives markets have developed over decades.

But what will be the WTI or Brent of AI compute, when technology keeps evolving with new chips, models and changing regional demand?

Bitcoin compute (hashrate) has an advantage here: one global network, one difficulty adjustment mechanism and a benchmark everyone can verify.

Bitcoin Difficulty is not a price, but it provides something derivatives markets need: a common, objective reference against which risk can be traded.

### X: the next adjustment

Few talk about Bitcoin hashrate.

After the last +5.9% adjustment (16-Oct), we are on track for another sharp increase.
We are 28% through this cycle, the estimate is about +4.7%, to 147.2T, around 29 October.

That is about 1.2 ZH/s in a 120 blocks average.

If average block time stays the same, the two adjustments in a row would reduce BTC mining revenues by ~10% in a month for the same machines.

### X: a market outside crypto

Since Oct 2022, listed utilities/network businesses — electricity, gas, water — are up 104%.

Autos & components: -2.7% (Ferrari, Pirelli, Brembo, Pininfarina)

Italian consumer brands: -8% over 5 years (Moncler, Brunello Cucinelli, De' Longhi, Geox).

This seems to be a combination of politics, energy prices, China and global conditions.

But the contrast is striking: in Italy, owning regulated infrastructure and concessions massively outperformed globally competitive industrial businesses.

What should be regulated for the benefit of everyone ends up to be a privilege for the few.

That's not a great signal for an economy that needs growth.

### LinkedIn: mining and AI

Bitcoin mining and AI are increasingly competing for the same resource: the energized megawatt.

From what we have seen so far, miners can move into AI but once they do, they rarely seem to come back.

In the meantime, hashprice just moved from roughly $31 to $36 in a single day.

AI landlord deals can generate multiples of mining's gross revenue per MW (in some cases up to 4x) but the conversion comes with much higher capex (potentially up to 10x), stronger credit requirements and often 10–15 year contractual commitments.

That 4x multiple is gross revenue, not net margin. The real economics become very site-specific once you take into account infrastructure costs, financing and long-term obligations.

So yes, "AI pays more", but it also costs more.

Miners accept that trade-off because converting to AI can lock in a long-duration contracted return. But in doing so, they give up part of the flexibility and upside that comes with Bitcoin mining. That optionality disappears under a long-term AI contract.

This is why I think risk management will become increasingly important for miners that remain focused on Bitcoin.

The key risk is not only BTC price. It is also network hashrate and difficulty, which directly determine Bitcoin miners revenues.

### LinkedIn: a thank-you

Ian Cain, you and the QUBIC Labs team are superstars. And the fact that it happened in Boston mattered.

I was part of the first QUBIC cohort and had access to exceptional mentors, support and guidance. Even after the accelerator program, I stayed in touch with the team and some of the other portfolio companies. We are like a family, where we celebrate each other's successes, share the same pains and become stronger together.

QUBIC also gave me a real connection to Boston.
The ecosystem, the quality of the people we met locally and the relationships I built with investors and other founders were really valuable.

I wish Doefin were at a later stage so that I could already be giving back to the ecosystem that helped me grow.

Thank you Ian, John and the QUBIC team for what you have built and for the opportunity you gave me.

### What they have in common

- A plain first line that goes straight to the subject: a number, a claim, or the reader's question.
- Exact figures with units, dates and qualifiers ("expected", "at the same hashrate", "all else equal"); estimates marked ("about", "~").
- A turn on "But" or "So yes".
- A named trade-off or limit ("gross revenue, not net margin", "does not cover every risk").
- Comparisons from commodities and markets the reader already knows.
- Opinions owned ("I think", "From what we have seen so far") and kept apart from company facts.
- One point at the end.


<!-- source: brand/matteo/edits.md -->
## Matteo's edits

Every draft Matteo has rewritten, with his version and what it teaches. This is the evidence behind `thinking.md`. Read it as worked examples: the draft on top is what a writer or a model produced, and the version under it is what the CEO wanted.

Source: the Doefin tone check, answered on 29 Oct 2026. Spelling, capitals, missing full stops and one missing article ("in a few minutes", E15) are corrected. Everything else is his wording; his comments are quoted exactly. Two entries are marked "attribution unconfirmed" where the export does not show clearly which words are his.

A lesson says what he changed. It does not guess why, unless he said why.

New edits go at the end, in the same shape, with the next number. `tools/add_edit.py` writes the entry for you; the learner procedure in `skills/doefin-voice/SKILL.md` says what to do next.

### Decisions he wrote himself

#### E01 · Doefin in one line · 29 Oct 2026

**Before**
> Markets for Bitcoin mining difficulty. / The first on-chain market on Bitcoin network difficulty. / On-chain derivatives on Bitcoin hashrate.

**After**
> Trade and hedge Bitcoin hashrate exposure through markets on mining difficulty.

**What it teaches:** He rejected all three options. He leads with the two actions and the economic exposure, and names difficulty last, as the mechanism. No category label and no "first".

#### E02 · Homepage headline · 29 Oct 2026

**Before**
> Markets for Bitcoin mining difficulty. / Trade Bitcoin mining difficulty. / What does the next difficulty rise cost you?

**After**
> Trade and hedge Bitcoin network hashrate.

**What it teaches:** The same two verbs. The headline names hashrate, the thing people are exposed to, not difficulty.

#### E03 · What we call what users do · 29 Oct 2026

**Before**
> Take a position / Trade / Hedge

**After**
> Use "Trade" for the action and "take the position" when explaining a market.

**What it teaches:** "Trade" on buttons and headlines. "Take a position" belongs in the explanation of how a market works.

#### E04 · LinkedIn About · 29 Oct 2026

**Before**
> Doefin builds decentralized derivatives on Bitcoin mining difficulty. With Doefin, miners can hedge revenue risk and BTC holders can earn native yield.

**After**
> Doefin provides markets for trading and hedging Bitcoin hashrate exposure.

**What it teaches:** He removed the category label ("derivatives") and the yield promise, and kept one sentence.

### Website lines

#### E05 · Homepage, under the headline · 29 Oct 2026

**Before**
> Each market asks one question: will difficulty be at or above a set level at a set block? Prices run from 0.01 to 0.99. Collateral is in BTC, and markets settle from public Bitcoin network data.

**After**
> Trade and hedge Bitcoin hashrate exposure through markets on mining difficulty. Each market asks whether difficulty will be at or above a set level at a specified Bitcoin block. Positions are funded and settled in cbBTC.

**What it teaches:** He turned the question into a statement, corrected a fact (the collateral is cbBTC, not BTC), dropped the price range and put the one-liner first.

#### E06 · Start with production · 29 Oct 2026

**Before**
> What changes when difficulty rises? For the same machines, a 5.92% rise means about 5.6% fewer coins until the next adjustment.

**After**
> A 5.92% rise in difficulty means about 5.6% less expected Bitcoin production from the same hashrate.

**What it teaches:** A statement, not a question. "Fewer coins" became "less expected Bitcoin production", and "the same machines" became "the same hashrate".

#### E07 · How it works · 29 Oct 2026

**Before**
> Review both outcomes before you enter.

**After**
> Choose a Bitcoin difficulty market, fund your account and buy Yes or No shares. Prices change as traders buy and sell.

**What it teaches:** Advice about the steps was replaced by the steps themselves. "Shares", and Yes and No in sentence case.

#### E08 · For miners, intro · 29 Oct 2026

**Before**
> Difficulty sets how many coins your machines earn. When it rises, the same fleet produces less. A Doefin market puts a price on that change.

**After**
> When Bitcoin mining difficulty rises, the same machines are expected to earn less Bitcoin, all else equal. Use Doefin markets to hedge that exposure.

#### E15 · v3 homepage, how it works · 29 Oct 2026

**Before**
> Review both outcomes before entering.

**After**
> Choose a market. Fund your account. Place a trade. All done in a few minutes.
>
> 1. Choose a Bitcoin difficulty market. Review the difficulty threshold and settlement block. Buy Yes if you expect difficulty to be at or above the threshold, or No if you expect it to be below. Prices change as traders buy and sell.
> 2. Fund your account and trade. Deposit cbBTC directly or use the integrated SwapKit to convert native BTC. Then choose your position and place your trade. cbBTC is a wrapped Bitcoin asset; it is not native BTC.
> 3. Sell or redeem. Place a sell order before settlement, or hold until the market resolves. A sale depends on available buyers and price. Each winning share redeems for 1 cbBTC; losing shares have no payout. Your profit or loss also depends on what you paid and any fees.

**What it teaches:** Three imperatives first. Then each step carries its own limit inside it: cbBTC is not native BTC, a sale depends on buyers, losing shares pay nothing. Attribution unconfirmed for the three steps: they may include v3 or docs text he pasted and edited (step 3's "A sale depends on available buyers" is the construction he changed to "Execution depends on" in E16).

A difficulty position may offset some mining losses, but does not cover every source of production or revenue risk.

**Before**

> Payout example
> Suppose you buy 0.01 Yes shares at 0.40 cbBTC per share. Your position costs 0.004 cbBTC.

#### E27 · v3 docs, risks and limitations · 29 Oct 2026

**Before**
> Review the limits of execution, payout, collateral and operational cover before using a market.

**After**
> Risks and limitations
> - Position risk. Losing shares have no settlement payout. You can lose the full position cost.
> - Exit risk. A sell order may not fill, or may fill only in part. The available price may be below the price you paid.
> - Collateral and technical risk. cbBTC is a wrapped Bitcoin asset with custody and redemption dependencies. Smart-contract, wallet, network or settlement failures can delay access to funds or cause losses.
> - Hedge limitations. A difficulty contract has a defined threshold and observation block. Its payout may not match your production losses. It does not directly cover changes in Bitcoin's price, energy costs, equipment performance or downtime.

**What it teaches:** A short label per risk, then the plain consequence. The hedge limit lists what it does not cover.

#### E29 · v3 glossary, mining difficulty · 29 Oct 2026

**Before**
> A number expressing how hard it is to find a valid Bitcoin block. Difficulty is the dial that holds that average steady as the total computing power pointed at the network changes.

**After**
> Mining difficulty
> A measure of how hard it is to find a valid Bitcoin block relative to the difficulty-one target.
> Difficulty adjusts every 2,016 blocks to target an average block interval of about ten minutes. At the same hashrate, higher difficulty reduces expected BTC production, all else equal.
>
> Difficulty-implied network hashrate
> The network hashrate implied by current difficulty if blocks arrive every ten minutes.
> It is calculated approximately as difficulty × 2³² ÷ 600 hashes per second. It translates difficulty into hashrate terms; it is not a live measurement of mining activity.
>
> 144-block estimated network hashrate
> An estimate of network hashrate based on work and elapsed time over a recent 144-block window.
> It responds to recent block timing and can fluctuate even when difficulty is unchanged. A 144-block window is not always 24 hours. Read it alongside the calculation method and observation time.

**What it teaches:** No metaphor ("the dial"). The technical reference, the adjustment rule, the effect on production, the formula, and for each related measure what it is not.

#### E30 · v3 article, reading a hashrate chart · 29 Oct 2026

**Before**
> Network hashrate is inferred from difficulty and block timing, rather than read from a register of mining machines.

**After**
> Bitcoin network hashrate is estimated from difficulty and block timing. It is not a direct count of Bitcoin mining machines.
> A difficulty-implied series assumes ten-minute blocks. A 144-block estimate uses recent block timing and can move more sharply. Neither is a live measurement. Check the method, time window and units before comparing charts.
> Doefin contracts reference mining difficulty at a specified block. A change in a hashrate estimate alone does not determine the contract outcome.

**What it teaches:** "Estimated" and "not a direct count" instead of an image. He ends by tying the topic back to the contract.

### Rules in his own words

Not edits, but what he wrote when asked. Quote these when a rule is challenged.

- On words to avoid: "Avoid unqualified promises such as 'guaranteed profit', 'risk-free', 'protect all revenues' or 'native yield'. Do not imply that a position directly delivers hashrate or covers every mining risk. Also avoid using the YES/NO position, but favour saying for example 'buy a position that pays out if difficulty is above X'."
- On words to use: "Use direct language: trade, hedge, hashrate exposure, mining difficulty, expected BTC production, market terms, position cost and payout. Use 'shares' in customer copy and explain once that they are position tokens."
- On what he disagrees with: "Use hashrate to describe the exposure and difficulty to describe what determines the outcome. Keep the distinction clear without repeating the full explanation in every section."
- On contractions: "Never use abbreviations. No: I'm, you're, there's. Yes: I am, you are, there is."
- On his own posts: "Write in my own voice using 'I'. Separate personal opinion from company facts. Apply the same standards for numbers, product claims and risk wording as company posts. Use agreed product language consistently."
- On the newsletter: "Lead with the news and explain why it matters. Cover difficulty markets, trading activity and network hashrate. Link sources and date estimates. Keep the subject line factual. State a publishing cadence only when the team has committed to it. Include relevant risk context when discussing positions."
- On research: "State the main finding early. Give figures a source, date, units and method. Distinguish observations, estimates, forecasts and opinion. Explain assumptions and material uncertainty. Assess forecast hits and misses consistently and make corrections visible."
- On tool text: "Say what the tool estimates. Label inputs and units, show assumptions and explain results in plain language. Distinguish BTC production from revenue and profit. Describe outputs as estimates and show material limitations near the result."
- On emails to partners and investors: "Open with the reason for writing, give the necessary context and end with one clear ask. For example: (1) what happened and deal flow, (2) what I am thinking, (3) idea or next steps, (4) product updates if any, (5) the ask."
- On what comes to him first: "Review new product claims, changes to settlement or collateral wording, financial examples, performance claims and legal or access language before publication. Routine content should use the agreed wording."
- On naming peers: "Name peers only in relevant, factual comparisons supported by current evidence. Do not imply endorsement or affiliation."
- On live prices in posts: "Yes, if possible use dated, time-stamped screenshots with the market and quote units visible. Do not imply that a displayed quote guarantees execution, liquidity or a return."
- On forecast misses: "Yes. Evaluate forecasts with the same method and make material misses and corrections visible."
- On investor and partner decks: "Use the same standards for evidence, product mechanics and risk claims. Adapt the depth and emphasis to the audience."
- On who signs the newsletter: "Use Doefin for company updates. Name the author when a piece presents a personal view."
- On other languages: "Hmmm, maybe yes."
- A writer he likes: Rapha Zagury (@RaphaZagury on X).
